title: Apple Vision Pro on “Life Support”: Gizmodo Reveals Troubled Future for Next‑Gen Headset
body:
Apple’s highly anticipated follow‑up to the Vision Pro headset appears to be teetering on the brink of cancellation, according to internal reports. Bloomberg analyst Mark Gurman, who has closely tracked Apple’s hardware pipeline, says the “next‑generation” mixed‑reality device is being kept alive only by a small group of engineers, while senior leadership has shifted its focus to more practical, lower‑cost wearables. The development team is reportedly operating on a “life‑support” mode, scrambling to justify the project’s existence amid dwindling resources and a market that has yet to embrace the original Vision Pro’s steep price tag.

The original Vision Pro, unveiled in early 2024, was marketed as a premium spatial computing platform that combined virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) capabilities. Priced at $3,499, the headset drew praise for its sophisticated optics, custom Apple silicon, and seamless integration with the broader Apple ecosystem. However, sales fell far short of expectations, and analysts have repeatedly warned that the device’s cost, limited app ecosystem, and bulky form factor could impede mass adoption. Those concerns now appear to be influencing Apple’s internal calculus on a successor.

Gurman’s assessment suggests that Apple’s senior executives have concluded the Vision Pro line will not generate the volume needed to justify a rapid, high‑end refresh. Instead, the company is reportedly channeling its mixed‑reality ambitions into a more modest, “consumer‑grade” headset that could be priced well below $1,000. Sources familiar with the project say the new device would prioritize comfort, battery life, and a streamlined software experience over the cutting‑edge hardware that defined the first model. This shift mirrors a broader industry trend, where competitors such as Meta and Sony are focusing on mid‑range devices that can attract a larger user base while still delivering compelling immersive experiences.

The internal debate at Apple reflects the tension between its tradition of premium, vertically integrated products and the economic realities of an emerging market. While the Vision Pro showcased Apple’s ability to engineer sophisticated optics and custom silicon, the headset’s high price limited its appeal to developers, enterprises, and a niche group of early adopters. By contrast, a lower‑priced headset could accelerate the growth of Apple’s AR/VR ecosystem, encouraging third‑party developers to create content and potentially unlocking new revenue streams through the App Store and subscription services. However, critics argue that diluting the brand’s premium positioning could erode the perceived value of Apple’s spatial computing vision.

Analysts also note that Apple’s broader product strategy may be influencing the decision. The company is currently rolling out new iterations of its flagship iPhone, Mac, and Apple Watch lines, all of which promise incremental upgrades rather than radical redesigns. In this context, a high‑risk, high‑cost headset that requires a separate ecosystem may be less attractive than a more modest device that can be integrated into existing product families. Moreover, Apple’s recent investments in ARKit, LiDAR sensors, and on‑device machine learning suggest the firm is still committed to augmenting reality, but perhaps through software‑first solutions that can run on existing hardware like iPhones and iPads.

If Apple proceeds with a scaled‑down headset, it could reshape the competitive landscape. A device priced under $1,000 would directly challenge Meta’s Quest line and could force other manufacturers to accelerate their own cost‑reduction strategies. Apple’s strong brand loyalty and its ability to leverage the App Store’s distribution network might give the new headset a decisive edge, especially if it offers seamless integration with services such as Apple Fitness+, Apple TV+, and iCloud. Conversely, a failure to deliver a compelling, affordable product could reaffirm doubts about Apple’s ability to dominate the mixed‑reality space.

Looking ahead, the fate of Apple’s next Vision Pro will likely hinge on how quickly the company can balance premium innovation with market‑driven pricing. While the current “life‑support” status underscores internal uncertainty, it also signals that a dedicated team is still fighting to keep the project alive. Should Apple succeed in delivering a more accessible mixed‑reality headset, it could spark a new wave of consumer interest and cement the company’s role as a pivotal player in the emerging spatial computing market. If not, Apple may retreat to a software‑centric approach, relying on its existing device portfolio to gradually introduce AR experiences. Either outcome will shape the trajectory of immersive technology for years to come.
